title: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark
description: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Loc
body: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London"."She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave."She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

schema.headline: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark

title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
description: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face courtImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock aft
body: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face courtImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attackByKaty WatsonAustralia correspondentReporting fromWangaratta, north-east Victoria and Phelan ChatterjeeA 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime". Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs."Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement."All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Helen Haines sits as an independent MP for the electoral division of Indi in Australia's state of VictoriaShe was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car."I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta."At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.The community, and country, remain in shock.At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

schema.headline: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend

title: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda
description: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert K
body: A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety."It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics."Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

schema.headline: Robert Kabera: Critic of Rwandan President Paul Kagame found beheaded in Uganda

title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors
description: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support"
body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the ChatGPT-maker, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and said a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.The 35-year-old engineer was deemed a flight risk and denied bail on Monday, pending a trial.The Saudi government did not respond to BBC requests for comment.Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official."Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued. US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".The FBI investigation is ongoing.Alfozan was scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

schema.headline: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, claims prosecutors

title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 73 security recruits, authorities say
description: More than 70 security personnel were killed in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa on Monday, local authorities sa
body: More than 70 security personnel were killed in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa on Monday, local authorities say.The Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.Monday's attack in Shabwa was the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground at the camp.Hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and were forced to transfer the most seriously wounded people to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based, Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency.Shabwa's media office initially reported that 53 people were killed and 200 injured in the attack. But on Tuesday, it said in a new statement that Governor Awad bin al-Wazir had been informed by an investigative committee that the death toll was now 73, with another 14 individuals reported missing.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 73 security recruits, authorities say

title: 'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says an overwhelming vote by people in Alberta to remain part of Canada is a "great result" for the country. Speaking to re
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney says an overwhelming vote by people in Alberta to remain part of Canada is a "great result" for the country. Speaking to reporters as he walked into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said he was "thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity" by rejecting a proposal to pursue separation through a binding referendum.Preliminary results indicate more than two-thirds chose Canada over a push for independence for the province, according to Elections Alberta, external.Monday's referendum was the result of a months-long campaign by separatists in the western Canadian province to get a public vote on the issue. Provincial leader Danielle Smith welcomed the initial results, commenting: "Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada."Premier Smith herself opposed the separatist push but said the public will for a vote was undeniable, and many supporters of her own political party - United Conservative Party -  were in the separatist camp. Smith said she would address Albertans later on Tuesday on the path forward for the province.In making the case for independence from Canada, many of the separatists said the oil-rich province's economic growth had been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.But those who opposed a breakup - including Carney - called for Canada to present a united front in the face of external pressures, including an ongoing trade war with the United States."They've chosen to build together," Carney said. "They've chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward, to move forward together, with purpose, high ambition."Carney added that he had spoken to Smith that morning and discussed "moving forward in the spirit of cooperative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities". Over the past year, the prime minister has worked with Smith on a number of shared goals, including pushing for an oil pipeline to the Pacific coast. At a pro-separatist watch party in Edmonton, the hum of upbeat chatter quickly quieted as those present saw the projected results.After overnight vote projections were published by Canadian broadcaster CBC and others, the mood soured. The watch party attended by the BBC packed up quickly, and people went home.One of the separatist leaders, Jeffrey Rath, struck a defiant tone, however, vowing that "our movement isn't stopping and we're continuing to move forward".Speaking to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme, Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary, said he saw Monday's vote as a "first step" which had taught the movement some "valuable lessons".Asked whether his movement would push to keep holding votes on independence until it got the result it wanted, he responded "why not?", and insisted that "the math and the economics" all added up on his side of the argument. Premier Scott Moe, from the province of Saskatchewan, said he was glad Albertans chose unity, but added that "there is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa".Pierre Poilievre, the leader of Canada's Conservative party and a member of parliament from Alberta, said on social media that "the promise of Canada is worth fighting for". "Now our focus must be on results in people's lives: affordable food and homes, safe streets, strong borders, and less immigration," he said. Smith called the vote after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition seeking a binding referendum on separation. The petition was blocked by a judge, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations people - however, Smith opted to go ahead with the ballot. Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The key question on Monday's voting paper asked: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"It's the first time a Canadian province has weighed the issue of separation since Quebec's two referendums, in 1980 in 1995. Both of those were unsuccessful, but Alberta separatists believe Quebec used the threat of independence to gain significant political leverage over Canada's central government.Smith said before the vote that if Albertans chose the remain option, a binding referendum on separation would not be held - at least, not while she was in power.

schema.headline: 'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism

title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
description: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" impo
body: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada  broke down in August.The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".The White House has been contacted for comment.Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry."These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338. Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.It  also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency."No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada."The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

schema.headline: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge

title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donal
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps".The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually.Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now"."Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said.He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia.Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink.Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals.Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war.Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia.On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly"."It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy"."We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

schema.headline: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo

title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
description: Figure caption, Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remainByNick BeakeEurope correspondentR
body: Figure caption, Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remainByNick BeakeEurope correspondentReporting fromMarseilleThunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors will come into force in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. An overnight curfew in parts of Paris, which came into force on Monday, has also been extended. Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away."It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.Image caption, Maryam (R) joined the protests on Saturday, which began in September over poor school conditions before escalating to cover broader issues such as the cost of livingMaryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen."It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began."But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact."Sometimes it goes too far."'An unheard-of level of violence'For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers."It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.Image caption, Hundreds of businesses were looted in several locations across the cityBlaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc."The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses."That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured."Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan.Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen."Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics."If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."Image caption, Chantal Bellanger said she was worried for young people rioting out of anger and despairWhile the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time"."We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair."It tugs at your heartstrings," she said."To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

schema.headline: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder

title: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media
description: A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke ou
body: A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.Marseille mayor Benoît Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The Préfecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend. Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".On Tuesday, Mélenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.The Rhône prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.

title: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?
description: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs p
body: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.Yet the photographs tell a different story. Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials. While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened. South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader. Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it. He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

schema.headline: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?

title: Fatima El Mansouri: What can Morocco's first female prime minister change for women?
description: The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Za
body: The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch. El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire. A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances. The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones. In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody. A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%."Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products."Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women."Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests."Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC."The latter cannot be understood without the former."Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important."It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system. The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts."I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC."Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."You may also be interested in:

title: Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters
description: Image caption, Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youthByLucy WilliamsonMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJ
body: Image caption, Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youthByLucy WilliamsonMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemWhen Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote."We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.Image caption, Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network."Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle."Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing.""Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav."I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice."Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."Image caption, Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next weekBen Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks."I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that."For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me."They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."Image caption, Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matterA series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians."The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media."Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats."Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram".Image caption, Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than othersYahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past."I love him," Mika told me."Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again."Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded."I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better."The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot.At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage.Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.Additional reporting by Morgan Gisholt Minard and Gidi Kleiman

schema.headline: Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
description: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.The second hand re-selling pla
body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend."The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage. Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses. Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast. "Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC."When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."France is one of Vinted's largest markets, along with the UK and Italy.The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

schema.headline: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale

title: Shakahola forest deaths: Paul Mackenzie's son says siblings were starved weeks before Kenya trial
description: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son saysImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie said educ
body: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son saysImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mackenzie said education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"ByBasma El AttiReporting fromNairobiUpdated 9 hours agoThe eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre."They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder. Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings."When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child. Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil"."I left school when I was seven," says Dan.Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life"."I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forestOn Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.Additional reporting by Thomas MukhwanaMore about the cult from the BBC:
